lead: A quantum channel is noisy. We can still ask how many classical bits it carries. Encode each message x into a quantum state ρ<sub>x</sub>, send it through the channel N, then measure the output to get y. The Holevo quantity χ limits how much information y gives about x. This matters for quantum links that must deliver ordinary data, keys and readout results.
prereq: You need: 5.3 for von Neumann entropy and 5.4 for coding limits.

blocks.text: Only a few universities teach this topic. Some syllabi call it “classical capacity of a quantum channel”. A message X is drawn from values x with probability p<sub>x</sub>. The encoder prepares ρ<sub>x</sub> on a qubit or larger system. The channel N maps it to N(ρ<sub>x</sub>). The decoder measures the output and reports Y. The pair (X,Y) is classical data.
χ = S(Σ<sub>x</sub> p<sub>x</sub> ρ<sub>x</sub>) − Σ<sub>x</sub> p<sub>x</sub> S(ρ<sub>x</sub>)
blocks.where: p<sub>x</sub> is the input probability; ρ<sub>x</sub> = N(ρ<sub>x</sub><sup>in</sup>) is the output state; S(ρ) = −Tr(ρ log₂ ρ) is the von Neumann entropy in bits; χ is the Holevo quantity in bits per channel use.

blocks.text: The Holevo bound says the accessible information I(X:Y) ≤ χ. Equality is possible in the limit of many copies for some channels. The classical capacity is C(N) = lim<sub>n→∞</sub> (1/n) χ<sub>max</sub>(N<sup>⊗n</sup>), where N<sup>⊗n</sup> means n parallel uses and χ<sub>max</sub> is maximized over input ensembles. The limit is needed because entangled inputs across uses can change χ at finite n.

For a bit-flip channel N<sub>p</sub>(ρ) = (1−p)ρ + p XρX, the input |0⟩ or |1⟩ is flipped with probability p. Equal inputs |0⟩, |1⟩ give χ = 1 − H₂(p), where H₂(p) = −p log₂ p − (1−p) log₂(1−p) is the binary entropy in bits. This equals the capacity of a binary symmetric channel.

For a depolarizing channel N<sub>p</sub>(ρ) = (1−p)ρ + p I/2, the state is replaced by the maximally mixed state I/2 with probability p. The same two inputs give χ = 1 − H₂(p/2), because each output state has eigenvalues 1−p/2 and p/2.
Set p=0.1 in the bit-flip case. Then H₂(0.1)=0.469 bits, so χ=C=0.531 bits per channel use. The channel carries a little more than half a bit per use, not one full bit.

figure.caption: A classical message X is encoded into quantum states, sent through a noisy channel, and decoded to Y. With a bit-flip error p=0.1 the channel block carries the one-use Holevo value 0.531 bits.

spec.title: Classical messages over a quantum channel
spec.aria: A classical message is encoded into quantum states, sent through a noisy quantum channel, and decoded into a classical message.

examples.question: A bit-flip channel flips its input bit with probability p = 0.1. The input bits are equally likely. Find the binary entropy H₂(0.1) and the Holevo quantity χ = 1 − H₂(0.1). Give units.
examples.answer: H₂(0.1)=0.469 bits and χ=0.531 bits per channel use.
examples.check:
import math
p = 0.1
H2 = -p*math.log2(p) - (1-p)*math.log2(1-p)
C = 1 - H2
print(round(H2, 3))
print(round(C, 3))

traps: The Holevo bound limits accessible information from one use of an ensemble; it is not automatically the full capacity when entangled inputs across many uses are allowed.
For a bit-flip channel use H₂(p); for a depolarizing channel use H₂(p/2). Mixing them is the commonest slip.
χ is in bits per channel use. Multiply by uses per second only if a rate in bits per second is asked.
Do not read χ as the entropy of the message X; it is a difference of output entropies.
The inequality is I(X:Y) ≤ χ, not χ ≤ I(X:Y).

quiz.q: Define the Holevo quantity χ for an ensemble {p<sub>x</sub>, ρ<sub>x</sub>}.
quiz.a: χ = S(Σ p<sub>x</sub>ρ<sub>x</sub>) − Σ p<sub>x</sub>S(ρ<sub>x</sub>), in bits per channel use.

quiz.q: Why is I(X:Y) ≤ χ only a one-use bound?
quiz.a: It limits information accessible from one channel use or one ensemble. Many uses can be combined with joint measurements and entangled inputs, so the capacity uses a limit.

quiz.q: A bit-flip channel has p=0.2 with equal inputs. Find χ.
quiz.a: H₂(0.2)=0.7219 bits, so χ=1−0.7219=0.2781 bits per channel use.

quiz.q: A depolarizing channel has p=0.2 with equal inputs |0⟩ and |1⟩. Find χ.
quiz.a: Each output has entropy H₂(p/2)=H₂(0.1)=0.469 bits, so χ=1−0.469=0.531 bits per channel use.

quiz.q: Why can entangled inputs require regularization in the capacity formula?
quiz.a: Entangled states across n channel uses can make χ(N<sup>⊗n</sup>) larger than n times the best single-use χ. The 1/n limit removes this finite-size effect and gives bits per use.

quiz.q: What do X and Y mean in the channel model?
quiz.a: X is the classical message chosen at the encoder. Y is the classical result of measuring the decoder output.

quiz.q: Write the classical capacity formula using χ.

beyond: Not for the exam. Classical capacity of quantum channels feeds into quantum network design, deep-space links and secure-key post-processing. Researchers study superadditivity, entanglement-assisted capacity and finite-blocklength rates. Search next for “Holevo-Schumacher-Westmoreland theorem”, “depolarizing channel capacity” and “entanglement-assisted classical capacity”.
